title: Can I include CEO salary in R&D tax credit calculations?
description: A CEO's salary counts for the federal R&D credit only for the share of W-2 wages spent on qualified research or first-line direct supervision.
summary: Yes, U.S. businesses can include a CEO's salary in federal R&D tax credit calculations under IRC §41, but only the portion of taxable W-2 wages allocable to qualified services: hands-on qualified research or first-line direct supervision. Executive administration and second-level oversight are excluded, so most CEO time won't qualify, and contemporaneous time records are essential.

body.text: Yes, U.S. businesses can include a CEO's salary in federal R&D tax credit calculations under IRC §41, but only the portion of taxable W-2 wages allocable to qualified services: hands-on qualified research or first-line direct supervision. Executive administration and second-level oversight are excluded, so most CEO time won't qualify, and contemporaneous time records are essential.
Prepared November 11, 2026. This report is informational and is not legal or tax advice.
Short answer

Yes, but only for the part of a CEO's wages that is allocable to "qualified services" as defined in Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §41(b)(2)(B), and only when supported by contemporaneous records that substantiate what the CEO actually did. A chief executive officer's corporate title or C-suite rank does not automatically make their wages eligible or ineligible for the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC §41; rather, the Treasury Regulations evaluate eligibility strictly based on the nature of the services actually performed by the individual employee. In practice, the strict regulatory definitions governing "direct supervision" (which is limited to immediate, first-line management) and the explicit statutory and regulatory exclusion of general administrative, financial, and personnel oversight mean that the vast majority of a typical CEO's working hours will not qualify. Any qualifying portion of a CEO's compensation must be rigorously separated from general executive duties and substantiated on an activity-by-activity and business-component-by-business-component basis.
1. The statutory and regulatory framework
1.1 Wages are a qualified research expense only when paid for qualified services

Under IRC §41(b)(2)(A)(i), in-house research expenses include "any wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by such employee." For purposes of calculating qualified research expenses (QREs), IRC §41(b)(2)(D)(i) explicitly provides that the term "wages" has the meaning given to such term by IRC §3401(a), which governs federal income tax withholding at the source. Consequently, only compensation that constitutes taxable wages subject to federal income tax withholding qualifies. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) on Qualified Research Expenses (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, IRC §41) explains that in practical terms, eligible in-house wages correspond to the taxable wages reported in Box 1 of Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement. Amounts paid to a CEO or corporate officer that are not subject to withholding under IRC §3401(a)—such as nontaxable fringe benefits, pre-tax elective deferrals to a §401(k) plan, non-qualified deferred compensation not yet includible in gross income, stock options that do not generate Form W-2 withholding wages, or S-corporation shareholder-employee pass-through distributions (reported on Schedule K-1 rather than as W-2 wages)—are strictly excluded from the QRE calculation even if the underlying work involved hands-on research services. Conversely, for a sole proprietor or a partner in a partnership who acts as CEO, IRC §41(b)(2)(D)(ii) extends the definition of wages to include "earned income" as defined in IRC §401(c)(2) to the extent allocable to qualified services performed in the trade or business.
1.2 The three categories of qualified services

IRC §41(b)(2)(B) strictly limits "qualified services" performed by an employee (including a corporate officer or CEO) to two statutory prongs: (i) engaging in qualified research, or (ii) engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities which constitute qualified research. Treasury Regulation §1.41-2(c) breaks these statutory prongs down into three distinct operational categories and defines the strict boundaries of each:

headers: What it means for a CEO (analysis)

cells: The actual conduct of qualified research, as in the case of a scientist conducting laboratory experiments (Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(1)).

Hands-on technical work personally performed by the CEO—such as writing source code, engineering CAD models, formulating chemical compounds, or directly designing and running experimental trials—can qualify on its own terms to the extent those activities satisfy the four-part test of IRC §41(d).

"The immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research (as in the case of a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments, but who may not actually perform experiments). 'Direct supervision' does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist" (Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(2)).

A CEO qualifies under this heading only when acting as the immediate, first-line manager of the engineers, scientists, or developers personally conducting the qualified research. Executive oversight of a Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Vice President of Engineering, or R&D directors who in turn supervise the researchers is treated as second-tier (higher-level) management and is strictly excluded.

Services in the direct support of either (i) persons engaging in actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research. It explicitly excludes "general administrative services, or other services only indirectly of benefit to research activities," and specifies that services of "officers engaged in supervising financial or personnel matters do not qualify as direct support of research." Furthermore, "Direct support does not include supervision" (Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(3)).

A CEO's financial management, budgeting, hiring, personnel evaluations, payroll approvals, and general corporate administration cannot be recast as direct support of R&D. Supervisory services must qualify, if at all, solely under the first-line management test of Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(2).

body.text: 1.3 Scientific background does not change the supervision rule

Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(2) is unambiguous that supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report is excluded from qualified services "even if that manager is a qualified research scientist." Analysis: Holding a Ph.D. in computer science or mechanical engineering does not convert second-level management (such as reviewing milestone reports from a VP of Engineering or chairing high-level product strategy meetings) into qualified direct supervision. However, a technically trained CEO is in no way barred from claiming time spent personally engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(1), or time spent directly supervising front-line researchers where no intermediate manager stands between the CEO and the technical bench (as often occurs in early-stage startups with flat organizational charts). The regulatory exclusion targets the organizational tier of supervision, not the officer's educational background or job title.
1.4 General management duties are excluded

Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(3) expressly excludes "general administrative services, or other services only indirectly of benefit to research activities" and explicitly states that "services of payroll personnel in preparing salary checks of laboratory scientists, of accountants in accounting for research expenses, of a janitor in general cleaning of a research laboratory, or of officers engaged in supervising financial or personnel matters do not qualify as direct support of research." Similarly, the IRS QRE Audit Techniques Guide instructs examiners to closely scrutinize high-salaried executives and officers whose titles and roles indicate substantial administrative, commercial, or executive responsibilities. At the same time, the ATG affirms that wage eligibility turns on the specific services an employee actually performs rather than on job title or formal job description alone. Neither IRC §41, the Treasury Regulations under §1.41-2, nor the IRS Audit Techniques Guide establishes a formal legal or statutory "presumption" specifically against CEO wages; rather, all taxpayers bear the general burden of proof under Tax Court Rule 142(a) and IRC §6001 to substantiate every claimed deduction and credit. Furthermore, while the specific examples of investor relations, fundraising, and M&A do not appear verbatim in Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(3), they fall squarely within the excluded category of general administrative and financial oversight activities (analysis).
2. Allocating a CEO's wages
2.1 The default time-ratio method

When an employee—such as a CEO who splits time between corporate governance and hands-on technical engineering—performs both qualified services and non-qualified services during a taxable year, only the portion of the employee's §3401(a) wages properly allocated to the qualified services may be included in in-house research expenses. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(d)(1), in the absence of another allocation method that the taxpayer can demonstrate is more appropriate, the amount of in-house research expense for that employee is determined by multiplying the total amount of wages paid or incurred for the employee during the taxable year by the ratio of the total time actually spent by the employee in the performance of qualified services to the total time spent by the employee in the performance of all services for the employer during the taxable year.
2.2 The "substantially all" (80%) rule for wages

Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(d)(2), if the amount of wages allocated to qualified services under the time-ratio method of §1.41-2(d)(1) constitutes at least 80 percent ("substantially all") of the wages paid or incurred by the taxpayer for an employee during the taxable year, then all (100 percent) of the services performed by that employee during the taxable year for the employer are treated as qualified services. Conversely, as emphasized in the IRS QRE Audit Techniques Guide, where an employee's ratio of qualified time to total working time falls below the 80 percent threshold, only the exact percentage of wages allocable to the actual qualified services performed may be claimed as a QRE. However, the IRS QRE Audit Techniques Guide specifically cautions examiners that higher-level research managers and executives typically perform qualified research or direct first-line supervision for only a minor fraction of their overall working hours, making a 100 percent CEO wage inclusion under the 80 percent rule an immediate focal point in IRS examinations.
2.3 Hypothetical worked example

Hypothetical, for illustration only. Suppose a startup CEO receives $300,000 in taxable Form W-2 Box 1 wages (as defined in IRC §3401(a)) during the calendar tax year. Contemporaneous project time logs, calendar records, and code-commit histories demonstrate that the CEO worked 2,000 total hours during the year. Of those 2,000 hours, 200 hours were spent acting as the immediate (first-line) supervisor of a software engineering team executing a qualifying process of experimentation on a new algorithm, and 100 hours were spent personally writing and testing experimental code. The remaining 1,700 hours included 400 hours overseeing the VP of Engineering and product managers (second-level supervision) and 1,300 hours on venture capital fundraising, board of directors meetings, financial management, and general corporate administration.

body.text: If the taxpayer attempted to add the CEO's 400 hours spent overseeing the engineering managers (rather than directly supervising the engineers performing the research), those 400 hours would be disallowed upon audit because supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report is expressly excluded from qualified services under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(2).
3. Substantiation: what the courts and Form 6765 require
3.1 Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner

In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. Mar. 7, 2023) (No. 21-3145, affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit held that "shortcut estimates of experimentation-related activities will not suffice. Something more, such as documentation of time spent on such activities, is necessary." The appellate court rejected arbitrary, unsubstantiated percentage estimates offered by management to satisfy the "substantially all" (80 percent) process-of-experimentation requirement under IRC §41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6). Little Sandy Coal concerned whether a commercial shipbuilder proved that substantially all of its development activities on vessel design projects constituted elements of a process of experimentation—not the allocation of CEO or C-suite executive compensation under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(d). Nevertheless, its rejection of uncorroborated, high-level percentage estimates applies directly by analogy to executive wage allocations: a CEO cannot simply estimate at year-end that "25% of my time was spent on R&D" without underlying factual documentation demonstrating the actual hours and activities performed (analysis).
3.2 Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner

In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (Docket No. 4759-22, filed December 23, 2024), the U.S. Tax Court evaluated whether a mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) consulting engineering firm's design work on three sample projects constituted qualified research under IRC §41(d) (where the claimed QREs consisted entirely of employee wages). The Tax Court held that none of the three trial projects satisfied the four-part statutory test, finding in particular that the taxpayer "failed to identify the specific information that was not available to PDG engineers at the start of the project" to establish technological uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design, and failed to demonstrate an evaluative process of experimentation. The court also noted that generic employee hour-sheet entries billed to broad project phases could not be connected to the specific technical uncertainties described in trial testimony. The trial in Phoenix Design Group specifically addressed whether the sample projects involved qualified research and excluded the quantification of QREs from the trial's scope; it did not adjudicate a separate legal standard for CEO wages.
3.3 George v. Commissioner

In George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10 (consolidated Docket Nos. 27494-16 and 21889-21, filed February 3, 2026), the U.S. Tax Court examined federal research tax credits claimed by the shareholders of an S corporation operating a large, vertically integrated poultry production business based on an after-the-fact research credit study. Judge Greaves disallowed credits for numerous poultry trials where retrospective assertions lacked contemporaneous support or conflicted with operational records, characterizing those claims as "an example of the chicken (research credit study) coming before the egg (research)." Conversely, the court allowed QREs for trials where contemporaneous settlement sheets, feed formulations, mortality logs, and spreadsheets verified that experimental flocks were actually tested to resolve genuine technological uncertainties regarding broiler health, nutrition, and antibiotic-free production. Furthermore, the court rejected the taxpayer's unsupported reconstruction of base-period QREs under the Cohan rule (Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)), holding that while estimates may sometimes be used when grounded in credible evidence, a lack of foundational evidence reduces the taxpayer to the lower 6 percent Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) rate under IRC §41(c)(4)(B)(ii).

In George, the taxpayer claimed only supply QREs (primarily experimental poultry feed and flock inputs) and did not claim any employee wage QREs at all because management determined calculating wage allocations was not worth the administrative effort—a point on which the Tax Court confirmed that supply QREs may be claimed independently without claiming wage QREs. Furthermore, for the qualifying trials, the court applied the process-of-experimentation test using contemporaneous operational records without demanding formal employee time logs. Nevertheless, George v. Commissioner strongly reinforces the overarching evidentiary principle applicable to CEO wage claims: retrospective reconstructions created during a post-year-end tax credit study cannot substitute for contemporaneous operational evidence proving that qualified research actually occurred, and courts will refuse to apply Cohan estimation where the taxpayer lacks credible foundational documentation (analysis).
3.4 Form 6765, Section G, Column 53 and Line 38

Under the IRS Instructions for Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities (Rev. December 2025, for use with the January 2025 revision of Form 6765), the IRS overhauled the reporting of qualified wages to give examiners immediate visibility into executive and supervisory compensation claims:

items: Line 38 (Officer Wages Disclosure): Section F / Part-level summary reporting on Form 6765 includes Line 38, which explicitly requires the taxpayer to report the total amount of officer wages (as defined for corporate tax reporting, such as Form 1120, Form 1120-S, or Form 1065 officer/partner compensation) that are included in total wage QREs reported on Line 42 (or the corresponding total wage line). This line allows the IRS to immediately flag returns where a disproportionate percentage of wage QREs stems from C-suite executives.

Section G (Business Component Information), Columns 50 through 53: Where Section G applies, taxpayers must break down qualified wages by each discrete business component. Specifically, Column 50 reports total in-house wage QREs for persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research; Column 51 reports total in-house wage QREs for persons engaging in the direct supervision of qualified research; Column 52 reports total in-house wage QREs for persons engaging in the direct support of qualified research; and Column 53 reports the total qualified wages for that business component (the sum of Columns 50, 51, and 52).

body.text: In IRS News Release IR-2025-99 (issued October 1, 2025) and the official Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), the IRS extended the transition period and confirmed that Section G is optional for all filers for tax year 2025 (tax years beginning before 2026). Section G becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (beginning in tax year 2026), subject to two major statutory/administrative exemptions under which Section G remains optional: (a) Qualified Small Business (QSB) taxpayers, as defined under IRC §41(h)(3), who elect to claim the reduced payroll tax credit, and (b) taxpayers with total QREs of $1.5 million or less and equal to or less than $50 million of gross receipts (determined at the controlled group level under IRC §448(c)(3) without regard to subparagraph (A)) claiming the research credit on an original filed return. Additionally, IR-2025-99 extended the 45-day transition period to perfect research credit claims for refund through January 10, 2027. Analysis: Because Column 51 isolates direct supervision wages by individual business component and Line 38 isolates total officer wages on the face of the return, any taxpayer claiming CEO wages for tax years beginning in 2026 or later (unless exempt from Section G) cannot rely on a lump-sum annual allocation; the CEO's direct conduct (Column 50) and first-line supervision (Column 51) wages must be tracked and mapped directly to each specific business component.
4. Methodology claims

items: Linking CEO time logs to architecture reviews, technical emails, or Jira tickets: Analysis: While IRC §41 and Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d) do not mandate any specific software system (such as Jira, GitHub, or calendar exports), linking time allocations to contemporaneous project artifacts directly addresses the evidentiary defects identified by the courts in Little Sandy Coal, Phoenix Design Group, and George.

Shrink-back rule and the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold: The "shrink-back rule" is a binding regulatory provision located at Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(b)(2). Under this rule, the four-part qualified research test of IRC §41(d)—including the requirement under IRC §41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6) that "substantially all" (at least 80 percent) of a business component's research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation—is applied first at the level of the discrete product or process as a whole. If the overall business component fails the test, the requirements are applied at the most significant subset of elements of the product or process, shrinking back progressively until either a qualifying subset of elements is reached or the most basic element of the product fails to qualify. Analysis: Taxpayers must carefully distinguish between two completely separate 80 percent rules in the regulations: (1) the 80% process-of-experimentation rule in Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6) (which determines whether a business component's activities constitute qualified research), and (2) the 80% "substantially all" wage rule in Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(d)(2) (which determines whether an individual employee's wages qualify at 100%). Satisfying the shrink-back rule on a sub-component under §1.41-4(b)(2) makes that sub-component a qualifying business component, but the CEO's wages are still limited under §1.41-2(d)(1) to the ratio of hours spent on qualified services relative to the CEO's total annual working hours across the entire company.

"Escalating" IRS enforcement specifically targeting executive wage misclassification: While the addition of Line 38 (officer wages) and Section G Columns 50–53 on the revised Form 6765 objectively demonstrates heightened IRS data collection on officer and supervisory wages, no separate formal IRS enforcement directive or statistical release opened for this report specifically announces an enforcement campaign isolated to CEO wage misclassification.

body.text: 5. Practical takeaways (analysis)

items: Focus on services performed, not executive title: Claim a CEO's Form W-2 (§3401(a)) taxable wages (or §401(c)(2) earned income for non-corporate entities) solely for hours where the CEO personally engaged in the actual conduct of qualified research under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(1) or acted as the immediate, first-line supervisor of the technical personnel performing the research under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(2).

Strictly exclude second-level supervision and executive administration: Exclude all hours spent supervising intermediate managers (such as CTOs, VPs of Engineering, or R&D directors) even if the CEO has an advanced scientific or engineering degree. Likewise, exclude 100 percent of time spent on corporate governance, investor relations, fundraising, M&A, financial budgeting, personnel reviews, and general administration under Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(c)(3).

Use exact fractional time allocations rather than the 80% wage rule: Allocate CEO wages strictly using the fractional time-ratio method of Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(d)(1) (qualified hours divided by total annual working hours). Treat the 80 percent "substantially all" wage rule of Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(d)(2) as practically unavailable for a functioning chief executive unless extraordinary, airtight contemporaneous evidence proves the CEO spent less than 20 percent of the year on all non-R&D executive responsibilities combined.

Maintain contemporaneous, component-level documentation: In light of Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (7th Cir. 2023), Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2024-113), and George v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-10), do not rely on retrospective year-end percentage estimates. Maintain contemporaneous time logs corroborated by dated technical artifacts (such as CAD revisions, code commits, experimental test protocols, or technical design reviews) that tie the CEO's hours to specific business components and establish the technological uncertainty that existed at the outset of the project.

Prepare for Form 6765 Line 38 and Section G reporting: Ensure payroll and R&D workpapers separately track officer wages for disclosure on Form 6765, Line 38, and—for tax years beginning after 2025 (unless exempt as a qualifying small taxpayer or QSB payroll-credit filer per IR-2025-99)—map the CEO's direct conduct wages (Column 50) and direct first-line supervision wages (Column 51) to each individual business component reported in Section G.
